article.title: Morning Soundings: The Number Is Not the Thing

capture.notes: Captured during the publication run from sources accessed on August 31, 2026.

signals.headline: An 89 percent estimate cannot identify one paper

canonicalSubject.name: LLM-assisted writing in PubMed Central papers

signals.canonicalClaim: A preprint estimated that 89 percent of sampled PubMed Central papers published in December 2025 contained signs of LLM-assisted writing or editing somewhere in their full text.
knownFacts: The analysis included 1,194,287 English-language PubMed Central papers dated 2017 through 2025 with Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion sections.
The estimator compared post-2022 frequencies of 379 LLM-associated marker words with trends projected from 2018 through 2022.
For random 255-word crops in December 2025, the estimated usage was 68 percent in Discussion sections and 32 percent in Methods sections.
uncertainties: The work was a preprint and had not completed journal peer review at capture time.
The estimate depends on the projected human-only vocabulary baseline remaining valid after 2022.
The method estimates prevalence across a corpus and cannot reliably classify an individual paper or distinguish translation, editing, and substantive generation.

evidence.notes: The authors provide methods, validation simulations, code, and corpus-level results in a public preprint; peer review and independent replication remain pending.

sources.title: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
Staggering 90% of biomedical papers now show signs of AI help

openQuestions: Will journal peer review or independent replication materially revise the estimate?
How much of the detected assistance consists of translation or editing rather than generation of scientific claims?
Can future estimators separate direct model use from human adoption or avoidance of model-associated vocabulary?

watchFor.description: Peer-reviewed publication or a revised preprint
watchFor.trigger: The authors publish a revised version, journal article, correction, or methodological response.

watchFor.description: Independent replication on PubMed Central or another scholarly corpus
watchFor.trigger: An independent group applies or tests the estimator and reports comparable prevalence results.

watchFor.description: Disclosure-policy changes tied to population-level evidence
watchFor.trigger: A major publisher or research body cites prevalence evidence when revising LLM-use disclosure rules.

trackingTerms: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing

disposition.reason: The estimate has clear revision and replication pathways, and its interpretation may affect scientific publishing policy.

signals.selectionReason: The study exposes the difference between a population fingerprint and an individual accusation while measuring a consequential change in scientific language.

signals.headline: Boat noise can remain after the boat has gone

canonicalSubject.name: Developmental motorboat-noise effects in spiny chromis

signals.canonicalClaim: In a controlled tank experiment, developmental exposure to motorboat-noise playback was associated with smaller juvenile spiny chromis and impaired escape responses measured after the playback had stopped.
knownFacts: The split-brood experiment exposed fish to motorboat noise or natural reef sound before hatching, after hatching, or during both periods for up to 78 days.
The predator-response test occurred after 24 hours without playback noise.
Fish exposed to motorboat noise as juveniles were about 7 percent shorter on average than fish exposed to reef sound as juveniles.
Among fish exposed to motorboat noise during both developmental periods, 68 percent responded to a simulated threat and 40 percent of responders moved toward it.
uncertainties: A tank playback experiment does not establish the size of the effect in a complex living reef.
The experiment did not isolate one mechanism connecting noise exposure to growth and escape behavior.
The population-level consequences of seasonal motorboat restrictions were not tested.

evidence.notes: The peer-reviewed article reports a controlled split-brood experiment; the institutional report accurately summarizes the published results.

sources.title: Motorboat noise playback during development limits reef fish growth and impairs predator responses with carryover effects
Motorboat noise stunts growth and impairs predator escape in reef fish, study shows

openQuestions: Do field studies find comparable growth and escape-response effects under real boat traffic?
Which physiological, behavioral, or parental-care pathway accounts for the carryover effect?
Would seasonal traffic limits measurably improve recruitment or survival?

watchFor.description: Field replication under natural reef traffic
watchFor.trigger: Researchers report growth, behavior, survival, or recruitment outcomes from fish exposed to measured boat traffic in the field.
A study identifies a physiological, feeding, sensory-development, or parental-care pathway for the carryover effect.

watchFor.description: Management trial or seasonal traffic restriction
watchFor.trigger: A reef authority implements and evaluates a breeding-season motorboat-noise intervention.

disposition.reason: The controlled finding has clear field, mechanism, and policy tests that could confirm, bound, or contradict its ecological significance.

signals.selectionReason: The experiment makes an invisible form of pollution legible as developmental history rather than a momentary disturbance.

signals.headline: Gold has a price; a hoard has a history

canonicalSubject.name: Theft of the Treasure of Villena

signals.canonicalClaim: Thieves removed most of the Treasure of Villena from the Villena Museum in a four-minute raid on August 27, 2026, and its recovery status remained unresolved in the public sources reviewed on August 31.
knownFacts: The museum alarm sounded at approximately 5:20 a.m., and officials said the thieves had departed by 5:24 a.m.
The Late Bronze Age hoard was discovered in 1963 inside a vessel buried in a dry streambed near Villena.
The collection included 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles, and other objects made from gold, silver, iron, and amber.
Villena's mayor estimated the gold content alone at approximately 1.7 million euros.
uncertainties: Immediate reports differed on the exact number and identity of objects taken while officials completed an inventory.
The reviewed public sources did not establish whether the objects remained intact, had entered an illicit market, or had been melted.
Europol's regional assessment describes a broader pattern but does not establish the actors, motive, or disposal route in this specific theft.

evidence.notes: Independent reporting relays named local officials and initial facts from an active investigation; Europol supplies authoritative regional context rather than case-specific attribution.

sources.title: Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist
Changing tactics, changing targets: the evolving nature of museum heists

openQuestions: Which objects were taken according to the completed official inventory?
Will investigators recover the objects intact?
Will the case produce documented security changes at Villena or other museums holding precious-metal heritage?

watchFor.trigger: Villena authorities or Spanish law enforcement publish a definitive stolen-object list, arrests, charges, or recovery information.

watchFor.description: Condition and provenance of recovered objects
watchFor.trigger: Any missing object is recovered and conservators report whether it remained intact or was altered.
Spanish cultural authorities or museums announce concrete security or display-policy changes linked to the theft.

disposition.reason: The case has a stable subject, unresolved recovery and preservation questions, and observable law-enforcement and museum-policy outcomes.

signals.selectionReason: The theft reveals a collision between commodity value and archaeological value: melting preserves the former by destroying the latter.
